title: Sickness Symptoms after vaccination
summary:
Systemic inflammatory processes, such as those that can occur during an infection or after a vaccination, are often accompanied by non-specific symptoms of illness. These symptoms, which are mediated by the immune system and are also referred to as ‘sickness behaviour’, are based on the effect of immune and pro-inflammatory messenger substances in the central nervous system. These so-called sickness symptoms typically include flu-like
symptoms such as increased sensitivity to pain, headache, aching limbs, fatigue and exhaustion. These symptoms are temporary and help us adapt our behaviour to the illness. They can also occur as a reaction to a vaccination against herpes zoster.
Herpes zoster, also known as shingles, is a painful viral disease caused by the reactivation of varicella zoster viruses that persist in the spinal cord or cranial nerves. The virus is the same one that causes chickenpox (varicella). The disease manifests itself through painful skin changes (blisters, redness, etc.) along a clearly defined area of skin. Herpes zoster can be treated effectively with antiviral medication, but in 10-20% of cases, a chronic pain syndrome can develop. The disease occurs more frequently in older people and is reactivated mainly under stress, when taking immunosuppressive drugs or if certain pre-existing conditions (such as diabetes mellitus or high blood pressure) are present. For several years, the Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) has recommended vaccination against herpes zoster (‘Shingrix’) for people aged 50 and over with pre-existing conditions and for healthy people aged 60 and over. According to the approval studies, Shingrix successfully reduces the risk of shingles and severe complications, especially post-herpetic neuralgia. The aim of this study is to better understand the mechanisms that influence non-specific disease symptoms such as fatigue and increased pain sensitivity after a herpes zoster vaccination. The study is a joint project of the Institute of Medical Psychology and Behavioural Immunobiology and the Clinics for Nephrology and Infectious Diseases.
The study includes two vaccination appointments (for the herpes zoster vaccination) and two follow-up examinations. On the first day of vaccination, you will receive the first dose of the Shingrix vaccine. As part of the study, you will be asked to complete several psychological questionnaires before and after the vaccination. A blood sample will also be taken and you will receive a prescription for ibuprofen (an anti-inflammatory medication), which you can redeem if necessary.
 After 48 hours, a follow-up examination with questionnaires and a blood sample will take place. This procedure will be repeated after 60 days with the second dose of the vaccine and then a second follow-up examination.
conditions: It is not a direct illness that is being investigated, but rather the effect of modulated symptom expectations resulting from appropriate medical information on the feeling of illness after vaccination.

interventions.name: Standard information (treatment as usual): Informed consent in a rational, matter-of-fact style by the physician. N=50 healthy patients.
Optimised education by study physician (elements: reframing of symptoms, use of primacy/recency effect, self-efficacy enhancement, empathetic interaction). N=50 patients

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with chronic conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, chronic kidney disease
Exclusion criteria:
Lack of ability to provide information, severe allergic reactions in the past, ibuprofen intolerance, acute infection, patients with a blood clotting disorder, history of immunosuppressive treatment or current immunosuppressive treatment according to a doctor's letter, and continuous use of immunosuppressants.
